title: Compassion in practice
hookLine: daya is the mother of dharma in the Japji

lines: THE EARTH ON A BULL'S BACK.
WHAT IS THE BULL STANDING ON?
cards: An old Indian picture of the world: the earth rests on the back of a great bull. It holds everything up. Solid, simple, done.
Then someone asks the question a child would ask: and what is the bull standing on? In the Japji, Guru Nanak asks it. In paraphrase: how much weight is on that bull, and what holds it up from below?
He doesn't throw the old picture away. He opens it up, and puts something surprising inside. Today: compassion in practice.

teach.h: THE BULL IS DHARMA, SON OF COMPASSION.
teach.b: First, the answer, in the sixteenth pauri of the Japji. In paraphrase: the bull is dharma, the son of compassion; it is contentment that patiently holds the earth in its place.
In the original, dhaul dharam daiaa kaa poot. The bull is righteous living, dharma. And dharma has a mother: daya, compassion.
Yesterday's santokh shows up too, as the thread that keeps it steady. Second, what that order means. Compassion comes first.

teach.h: RULES BORN FROM CARING STAY WARM.
teach.b: Rules, duties, right conduct: all of it is born from caring. If dharma loses its mother, it becomes rules that can be kept coldly, even cruelly. If it keeps her, the rules stay warm.
Third, the same pairing, in a salok you met early on this path. In Asa di Var, offered a ritual sacred thread, Guru Nanak describes the only thread he'd wear.
In paraphrase: make compassion the cotton, contentment the thread, self-restraint the knots, and truth the twist; that is the thread for the soul, and if you have it, put it on me.
Compassion again sits at the bottom, the raw cotton everything is spun from. Fourth, in practice. Compassion here isn't a mood.
It's what moves a hand: a langar ladle, a meal carried to a neighbor, a hard truth said gently instead of cruelly.

It isn't softness either; a Sikh may stand firm against wrong and still let compassion set the tone. When a rule and a person seem to pull in different directions, ask the mother before you ask the son.

how: Sikhs speak of daya, compassion, as a core virtue and express it in seva: serving langar, caring for the sick and helping those in need, whoever they are.

o: a rule to forgive any wrong without question
caring that moves a hand, the root of right conduct
feeling sorry for someone from a safe distance

games.q: what's inside the Japji's bull: tap the pairs.
p: the thread that holds the earth

s: in the Japji, Guru Nanak simply repeats that the earth sits on a bull
he asks what holds the bull up, and answers: the bull is dharma, son of compassion.
in Asa di Var, Guru Nanak's thread for the soul is spun from compassion
compassion the cotton, contentment the thread, self-restraint the knots, truth the twist.
compassion in Sikh teaching means never standing firm
a Sikh may stand firm against wrong and still let compassion set the tone.

games.q: you're hearing the old picture: the earth rests on a bull. what does Guru Nanak do with it in the Japji?
o: ask what the bull stands on, and say it is dharma, son of compassion.
reject it as nonsense and move on.
games.why: he opens the old picture up: the bull is dharma, born of daya, and contentment holds the earth in place.

practice: Bring to mind one person you'll see or talk to today: someone tired, maybe, or difficult, or easy to overlook. Breathe in and ask what it's like to be them today; breathe out and let a little of the answer reach you.
Then let one small act that would help them come clear.

wordCard.voice: Compassion in practice. Daya: in the Japji, the mother of dharma; right conduct is born from caring, and caring shows up as something done. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: daya, compassion; in the Japji, the mother of dharma.

carryVoice: Your line: compassion first. In the Japji, dharma's mother is daya, compassion. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Ang 3 (Japji, pauri 16: dhaul dharam daiaa kaa poot, santokh thaap rakhiaa jin soot)
Ang 471 (Asa di Var, salok of Guru Nanak: daiaa kapaah santokh soot jat gandhee sat vatt)
